##### 3-1 Quaternary complexes

Figure 11 depicts a typical 3-1 quaternary complex. Such a complex is uniquely characterized by the length of its oligomers, $L_{C},L_{W,1},L_{W,2},L_{W,3}$, as well as their relative position to each other denoted by the alignment indices $i,j$, and $k$. All positions within the ternary complex are measured relative to the left end of the C strand. Any W strand needs to have at least one nucleotide of overlap with the C strand, but two W strands must never occupy the same position on the C strand. Consequently, the alignment indices fall within the intervals,

$$
i\in[−(L_{W,1}−1),L_{C}−L_{W,1}−L_{W,2}−1],    j\in[i+L_{W,1},L_{C}−L_{W,2}−1],   and   k\in[j+L_{W,2},L_{C}−1].
$$

There are two dangling ends (left and right) and potentially two gaps between the W strands: one gap between W1 and W2 and another one between W2 and W3. The following boolean variables indicate the presence/absence of the respective dangling ends,

$$
d_{l}={0if i=0,1otherwise,   d_{m1}={0if i+L_{W,1}=j,1otherwise,d_{m2}={0if i+L_{W,2}=k,1otherwise,  d_{r}={0if k+L_{W,3}=L_{C},1otherwise.
$$

The length of the hybridization regions is given by

$$
L_{o,1}=i+L_{W,1}−max(i,0),    L_{o,2}=L_{W,2},   and   L_{o,3}=min(L_{C},k+L_{W,3})−k.
$$

Following the same reasoning as in the case of ternary complexes, the energy equals

$$
E=\gamma(L_{o,1}+L_{o,2}+L_{o,3}−3)+\gamma(1−d_{m1})+\gamma(1−d_{m2})+\frac{\gamma}{2}(d_{l}+d_{r}+2d_{m1}+2d_{m2}).
$$

Similarly, the combinatorial multiplicity of 3-1 quaternary complexes is constructed using the same reasoning as in the case of ternary complexes,

$$
C(L_{C},L_{W,1},L_{W,2},L_{W,3},i,j,k)=C(L_{C})\times[\frac{C(L_{W,1})}{4^{L_{o,1}}}1(L_{o,1}<L_{U}^{min})+1(L_{o,1}\geqL_{U}^{min})]\times[\frac{C(L_{W,2})}{4^{L_{o,2}}}1(L_{o,2}<L_{U}^{min})+1(L_{o,2}\geqL_{U}^{min})]\times[\frac{C(L_{W,3})}{4^{L_{o,3}}}1(L_{o,3}<L_{U}^{min})+1(L_{o,3}\geqL_{U}^{min})].
$$

As 3-1 quaternary complexes are not symmetric under rotation, no symmetry correction of the combinatorial multiplicity is necessary.

##### Left-tilted 2-2 quaternary complexes

A 2-2 quaternary complex is comprised of two C strands and two W strands. We call a 2-2 complex left-tilted if strand W1 is connected to strand W2 via strand C1 (Figure 12A). The lengths of the oligomers are called $L_{W,1},L_{W,2},L_{C,1}$, and $L_{C,2}$. The positions of the strands relative to each other are governed by the alignment indices. All positions are measured relative to the position of the left end of strand C1. The alignment indices may take on the following values,

$$
i\in[−(L_{W,1}−1),L_{C,1}−L_{W,1}−1],    j\in[i+L_{W,1},L_{C,1}],   and   k\in[L_{C,2},j+L_{W,2}−1].
$$

The complex can have dangling ends on the right and on the left end of the complex; the presence of these dangling ends is indicated by the boolean variables $d_{l}$ and $d_{r}$. Moreover, two gaps are possible: There might be a gap between strands W1 and W2, or a gap between C1 and C2. The respective boolean variables read

$$
d_{l}={0if i=0,1otherwise,d_{m1}={0if i+L_{W,1}=j,1otherwise,d_{m2}={0if L_{C,1}=k,1otherwise,d_{r}={0if j+L_{W,2}=k+L_{C,2},1otherwise.
$$

We refer to the hybridization region of strand W1 and C1 as overlap region 1, to the hybridization region of strand W2 and C1 as overlap region 2 and to the hybridization region of strand W2 and C2 as overlap region 3. The length of these hybridization regions is computed via

$$
L_{o,1}=i+L_{W,1}−max(i,0),    L_{o,2}=L_{C,1}−j,   and   L_{o,3}=min(j+L_{W,2},k+L_{C,2})−k.
$$

Given the length of the hybridization region as well as the presence/absence of dangling ends, we can compute the hybridization energy,

$$
E=\gamma(L_{o,1}+L_{o,2}+L_{o,3}−3)+\gamma(1−d_{m1})+\gamma(1−d_{m2})+\frac{\gamma}{2}(d_{l}+d_{r}+2d_{m1}+2d_{m2}).
$$

The combinatorial multiplicity of a left-tilted 2-2 quaternary complex is constructed using the same reasoning as in the case of a 3-1 complex,

$$
C(L_{C,1},L_{C,2},L_{W,1},L_{W,2},i,j,k)=C(L_{C})\times[\frac{C(L_{W,1})}{4^{L_{o,1}}}1(L_{o,1}<L_{U}^{min})+1(L_{o,1}\geqL_{U}^{min})]\times[\frac{C(L_{W,2})}{4^{L_{o,2}}}1(L_{o,2}<L_{U}^{min})+1(L_{o,2}\geqL_{U}^{min})]\times[\frac{C(L_{C,1})}{4^{L_{o,3}}}1(L_{o,3}<L_{U}^{min})+1(L_{o,3}\geqL_{U}^{min})].
$$

To prevent double-counting the same quaternary complex, we include either the complex or its rotated representation in the container of possible complexes, but not both. If the complex is symmetric under rotation, we multiply the combinatorial multiplicity by $1/2$. Given a left-tilted 2-2 quaternary complex $(L_{C,1},L_{C,2},L_{W,1},L_{W,2},i,j,k)$, we can compute the corresponding rotated complex $(L_{C,1}^{rot},L_{C,2}^{rot},L_{W,1}^{rot},L_{W,2}^{rot},i^{rot},j^{rot},^{rot})$ by applying a linear map. The mapping of the oligomer lengths is illustrated in Figure 12B. We see that strand C2 after rotation corresponds to strand W1 before rotation, implying that $L_{C,2}^{rot}=L_{W,1}$. The same reasoning can be applied to all strands leading to the map,

$$
L_{C,1}^{rot}=L_{W,2},    L_{C,2}^{rot}=L_{W,1},    L_{W,1}^{rot}=L_{C,2},   and   L_{W,2}^{rot}=L_{C,1}.
$$

In order to compute the map of the alignment indices under rotation, we need to express the relative positions of the strands with respect to the position of strand C1 after rotation, which corresponded to W2 before rotation. For example, $|i^{rot}|$ corresponds to the number of nucleotides by which strand C2 (before rotation) protrudes beyond strand W2 (before rotation). Expressed in terms of variables before rotation, this distance may be written as $k+L_{C,2}−jL_{W,2}$. Analogous relations can be derived for all alignment indices,

$$
i^{rot}=j−k+L_{W,2}−L_{C,2},    j^{rot}=j+L_{W,2}−L_{C,1},   and   k^{rot}=j−i+L_{W,1}−L_{W,2}.
$$

##### Right-tilted 2-2 quaternary complexes

A 2-2 quaternary complex is called right-tilted if strand W1 is connected to strand W2 via strand C2 (Figure 13). As in the case of the left-tilted 2-2 complex, the oligomer lengths are again called $L_{W,1},L_{W,2},L_{C,1}$ and $L_{C,2}$, but the values of the alignment indices that are possible for the right-tilted quaternary complex differ from the ones of the left-tilted complex,

$$
i\in[L_{C,1}−L_{W,1}−1,L_{C,1}−1],    j\in[L_{C,1},i+L_{W,1}−1],   and   k\in[i+L_{W,1},k+L_{C,2}−1].
$$

Note that the range of $i$ is chosen such that at least one nucleotide of strand W1 always extends to the right beyond the end of strand C1, allowing for a hybridization region between strand C2 and W1. The boolean variables denoting the presence/absence of dangling ends read

$$
d_{l}={0if i=0,1otherwise,d_{m1}={0if i+L_{W,1}=j,1otherwise,d_{m2}={0if L_{C,1}=k,1otherwise,d_{r}={0if j+L_{W,2}=k+L_{C,2},1otherwise.
$$

The length of the overlap regions is given by

$$
L_{o,1}=L_{C,1}−max(i,0),    L_{o,2}=i+L_{W,1}−k,   and   L_{o,3}=min(k+L_{C,2},j+L_{W,2})−j.
$$

Like in the case of left-tilted 2-2 quaternary complexes, the total hybridization energy is computed via

$$
E=\gamma(L_{o,1}+L_{o,2}+L_{o,3}−3)+\gamma(1−d_{m1})+\gamma(1−d_{m2})+\frac{\gamma}{2}(d_{l}+d_{r}+2d_{m1}+2d_{m2}),
$$

and the combinatorial multiplicity via

$$
C(L_{C,1},L_{C,2},L_{W,1},L_{W,2},i,j,k)=C(L_{C})\times[\frac{C(L_{W,1})}{4^{L_{o,1}}}1(L_{o,1}<L_{U}^{min})+1(L_{o,1}\geqL_{U}^{min})]\times[\frac{C(L_{W,2})}{4^{L_{o,2}}}1(L_{o,2}<L_{U}^{min})+1(L_{o,2}\geqL_{U}^{min})]\times[\frac{C(L_{C,1})}{4^{L_{o,3}}}1(L_{o,3}<L_{U}^{min})+1(L_{o,3}\geqL_{U}^{min})].
$$

We include either the quaternary complex or its rotated representation in the list of possible complexes to avoid double-counting. Moreover, the combinatorial multiplicity is divided by 2 if the complex is symmetric under rotation. It turns out that the rotation map for the right-tilted 2-2 quaternary complex is identical to the one of the left-tilted 2-2 complex,

$$
L_{C,1}^{rot}=L_{W,2},    L_{C,2}^{rot}=L_{W,1},    L_{W,1}^{rot}=L_{C,2},    L_{W,2}^{rot}=L_{C,1},i^{rot}=j−k+L_{W,2}−L_{C,2},    j^{rot}=j+L_{W,2}−L_{C,1},   and   k^{rot}=j−i+L_{W,1}−L_{W,2}.
$$

### Numerical solution of the (De)hybridization equilibrium in the adiabatic approach

Based on the list of complexes constructed in the previous section, we can compute the equilibrium concentration of strands and complexes reached in the (de)hybridization equilibrium. In the following, we denote the concentration of a coarse-grained oligomer with length $L$ as $c(L)$, and the concentration of an oligomer with length $L$ and known sequence as $c_{s}(L)$. Recall that we assumed that all sequences of a given length that are compatible with the circular genome are equally likely in the pool. Thus, the concentration of the coarse-grained oligomer and the concentration of an oligomer with specified sequence are related by the combinatorial multiplicity,

$$
c(L)=C(L)c_{s}(L).
$$

In order to compute the concentration of a complex based on the concentration of single strands, we make use of the law of mass action. The concentration of a specific sequence realization of a complex is computed as the product of concentrations of the strands forming the complex divided by the dissociation constant $K_{d}$,

$$
c_{s}(L→,i→)=\frac{1}{K_{d}(L→,i→)}\prodjc_{s}(L_{j}).
$$

Here, $L→$ is the vector denoting the lengths of the strands comprising the complex, and $i→$ are the alignment indices. The dissociation constant is set by the hybridization energy, $ΔG$, of the complex,

$$
K_{d}(L→,i→)=(c^{∘})^{n−1}exp⁡(\betaΔG),
$$

where $c^{∘}=1M$ is the standard concentration. Just as in the case of single strands, the concentration of the sequence-independent coarse-grained complex is related to the concentration of a complex with specific sequence realization via the combinatorial prefactor,

$$
c(L→,i→)=C(L→,i→)c_{s}(L→,i→).
$$

It can be useful to combine the combinatorial multiplicity and the dissociation constant into a single effective association constant,

$$
K_{a}(L→,i→)=\frac{C(L→,i→)}{K_{d}(L→,i→)}.
$$

Note that the effective association constant including the combinatorial multiplicity is denoted by $K_{a}$ (in curly font), while the association constant without combinatorial multiplicity is denoted $K_{a}=K_{d}^{−1}$ (in regular font).

In the adiabatic approach, we study the behavior of the system on timescales that are long enough for the system to reach the (de)hybridization equilibrium, but too short for templated ligation events to take place. Therefore, the length of the oligomers is expected not to change throughout the equilibration process, and we need to introduce a separate mass conservation law for each coarse-grained oligomer, that is each oligomer length, that is included in the pool. For each length, the concentration of single-stranded coarse-grained oligomers of length $L$ and the concentration of coarse-grained oligomers of length $L$ bound in a complex need to add up to their total concentration $c(L)$ set by the initial condition,

$$
c^{eq}(L)+\sum(L→,i→)|∃js.t.L→_{j}=Lc^{eq}(L→,i→)=c^{tot}(L).
$$

In this equation, $(L→,i→)|∃js.t.L→_{j}=L$ denotes the summation over all complexes that contain at least one strand of length $L$. Note that we referred to the total concentration of oligomers of length $L$ as $c(L)$ in the main text, but for clarity, we use $c^{tot}(L)$ in the following.

Combining the mass conservation requirement with the mass action law gives a set of coupled polynomial equations. The number of equations equals the number of distinct oligomer lengths included in the pool. The polynomial equations are of degree 4, as quaternary complexes are the largest complexes to be accounted for and their concentrations equal the product of the four strands comprising the complex. We determine the equilibrium concentrations by finding the root of this set of fourth-degree polynomial equations using the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm.

### Computing replication observables based on the adiabatic approach

As we are not modeling templated ligation events explicitly in the adiabatic approach, we compute replication observables based on the equilibrium concentration of complexes that are in a configuration which allows for a templated ligation reaction to happen. Templated ligations are possible if two strands in the complex are adjacent to each other, that is there is no gap in between two oligomers that are hybridized to the same template strand (Figure 14). Recall that the absence of a gap between two oligomers in the complex implies that the dangling end indicator variable $d_{m}=0$. The length of the product strand P is equal to the sum of the lengths of the two educt strands E1 and E2, $L_{p}=L_{e,1}+L_{e,2}$. We can use the information about the length of the product strand to compute the yield of replication. By definition, the yield equals the fraction of nucleotides used to form VCG oligomers, that is strands that are at least $L_{U}$ long,

$$
y=\frac{#nucleotidesincorporatedinVCGoligomers}{#incorporatednucleotides}.
$$

**Figure 14.:** The strands E1 and E2 are adjacent to each other, such that a covalent bond can form between their ends. The length of the product strand, $L_{p}$, is set by the length of the educt strands, $L_{e,1}$ and $L_{e,2}$. The likelihood for the complex to form a product oligomer whose sequence is compatible with the true circular genome, $p_{corr}$, is determined by the length of the educts and the length of their hybridization region with the template. The parts of the complex shown with hatching do not affect $p_{corr}$.

We can express this quantity in terms of the equilibrium concentration of complexes facilitating templated ligation,

$$
y=\frac{\sum(L→,i→)|(d_{m}=0∧L_{e,1}+L_{e,2}\geqL_{U}^{min}) min(L_{e,1},L_{e,2})c^{eq}(L→,i→)}{\sum(L→,i→)|d_{m}=0 min(L_{e,1},L_{e,2})c^{eq}(L→,i→)}.
$$

$(L→,i→)|(d_{m}=0∧L_{e,1}+L_{e,2}\geqL_{U}^{min})$ denotes the summation over all complexes, in which (i) the strands E1 and E2 are adjacent to each other, that is $d_{m}=0$, and (ii) the length of the product $L_{e,1}+L_{e,2}\geqL_{U}^{min}$. We multiply the equilibrium concentration by the length of the shorter educt strand to account for the number of incorporated nucleotides in line with the definition of the yield (Equation 7).

In order to compute the fidelity of replication, we need to distinguish between product oligomer sequences that are compatible with the genomes (correct sequences) and sequences that are incompatible with the genome (false sequences). As we do not know about the details of the sequences due to the coarse-grained representation of the complexes, we need to invoke a combinatorial argument to determine the fraction of correct products. To this end, we compare the number of product sequences that might be produced in a complex of given oligomer lengths and alignment indices to the number of correct products associated with the same complex configuration. The combinatorial multiplicity of the products that could be produced by a complex of given configuration is set by the combinatorial multiplicity of the possible templates, $C(L_{o,1}+L_{o,2})$, multiplied by the multiplicity of the educt strands hybridizing to the template with given lengths of the hybridization regions, $L_{o,1}$ and $L_{o,2}$,

$$
C(possible products)=C(L_{o,1}+L_{o,2})\frac{C(L_{e,1})}{C(L_{o,1})}\frac{C(L_{e,2})}{C(L_{o,2})}.
$$

The multiplicity of correct products equals the combinatorial multiplicity of strands that have the same length as the product,

$$
C(correct products)=C(L_{e,1}+L_{e,2}).
$$

This implies that the probability for a complex of given shape $(L→,i→)$ to form a correct product is given by

$$
p_{corr}(L→,i→)=\frac{C(correct products)}{C(possible products)}=\frac{C(L_{e,1}+L_{e,2})C(L_{o,1})C(L_{o,2})}{C(L_{o,1}+L_{o,2})C(L_{e,1})C(L_{e,2})}.
$$

Using this probability, we can compute the fidelity of replication,

$$
f=\frac{\sum(L→,i→)|(d_{m}=0∧L_{e,1}+L_{e,2}\geqL_{U}^{min}) p_{corr}(L→,i→)min(L_{e,1},L_{e,2})c^{eq}(L→,i→)}{\sum(L→,i→)|(d_{m}=0∧L_{e,1}+L_{e,2}\geqL_{U}^{min}) min(L_{e,1},L_{e,2})c^{eq}(L→,i→)}
$$

as well as the replication efficiency,

$$
η=\frac{\sum(L→,i→)|(d_{m}=0∧L_{e,1}+L_{e,2}\geqL_{U}^{min}) p_{corr}(L→,i→)min(L_{e,1},L_{e,2})c^{eq}(L→,i→)}{\sum(L→,i→)|d_{m}=0 min(L_{e,1},L_{e,2})c^{eq}(L→,i→)}.
$$

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.104043.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.104043.3.sa1)

Summary:

This is an interesting theoretical study examining the viability of Virtual Circular Genome (VCG) model, a recently proposed scenario of prebiotic replication in which a relatively long sequence is stored as a collection of its shorter subsequences (and their compliments). It was previously pointed out that VCG model is prone to so-called sequence scrambling which limits the overall length of such a genome. In the present paper, additional limitations are identified. Specifically, it is shown that VCG is well replicated when the oligomers are elongated by sufficiently short chains from "feedstock" pool. However, ligation of oligomers from VCG itself results in a high error rate. I believe the research is of high quality and well written. However, the presentation could be improved and the key messages could be clarified.

(1) It is not clear from the paper whether the observed error has the same nature as sequence scrambling

(2) The authors introduce two important lengths LS1 and LS2 only in the conclusions and do not explain enough which each of them is important. It would make sense to discuss this early in the manuscript.

(3) It is not entirely clear why specific length distribution for VCG oligomers has to be assumed rather than emerged from simulations.

(4) Furthermore, the problem has another important length, L0 that is never introduced or discussed: a minimal hybridization length with a lifetime longer than the ligation time. From the parameters given, it appears that L0 is sufficiently long (~10 bases). In other words, it appears that the study is done is a somewhat suboptimal regime: most hybridization events do not lead to a ligation. Am I right in this assessment? If that is the case, the authors might want to explore another regime, L0

Strengths:

High-quality theoretical modeling of an important problem is implemented.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.104043.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.104043.3.sa2)

Summary:

This important theoretical and computational study by Burger and Gerland attempts to set environmental, compositional, kinetic, and thermodynamic constraints on the proposed virtual circular genome (VCG) model for the early non-enzymatic replication of RNA. The authors create a solid kinetic model using published kinetic and thermodynamic parameters for non-enzymatic RNA ligation and (de)hybridization, which allows them to test a variety of hypotheses about the VCG. Prominently, the authors find that the length (longer is better) and concentration (intermediate is better) of the VCG oligos have an outsized impact on the fidelity and yield of VCG production with important implications for future VCG design. They also identify that activation of only RNA monomers, which can be achieved using environmental separation of the activation and replication, can relax the constraints on the concentration of long VCG component oligos by avoiding the error-prone oligo-oligo ligation. Finally, in a complex scenario with multiple VCG oligo lengths, the authors demonstrate a clear bias for the extension of shorter oligos compared to the longer ones. This effect has been observed experimentally (Ding et al., JACS 2023) but was unexplained rigorously until now. Overall, this manuscript will be of interest to scientists studying the origin of life and the behavior of complex nucleic acid systems.

Strengths:

- The kinetic model is carefully and realistically created, enabling the authors to probe the VCG thoroughly.

- Fig. 6 outlines important constraints for scientists studying the origin of life. It supports the claim that the separation of activation and replication chemistry is required for efficient non-enzymatic replication. One could easily imagine a scenario where activation of molecules occurs, followed by their diffusion into another environment containing protocells that encapsulate a VCG. The selective diffusion of activated monomers across protocell membranes would then result in only activated monomers being available to the VCG, which is the constraint outlined in this work. The proposed exclusive replication by monomers also mirrors the modern biological systems, which nearly exclusively replicate by monomer extension.

- Another strength of the work is that it explains why shorter oligos extend better compared to the long ones in complex VCG mixtures. This point is independent of the activation chemistry used (it simply depends on the kinetics and thermodynamics of RNA base-pairing) so it should be very generalizable.

results.result: The Virtual Circular Genome (VCG) is a prebiotic replication scenario proposed by Zhou et al. (2021) in which genetic information is stored in a pool of oligomers shorter than the circular genome they collectively encode, with each oligomer acting as both template and primer.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C32, C33, C34, C35, C66, and C67 consistently describe the VCG scenario as proposed by Zhou et al. (2021), with proper citation. The description is coherent and well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Three competing types of template-directed ligation reactions emerge in the VCG: F+F ligations (producing short products), F+V ligations (typically correct), and V+V ligations (often erroneous). Erroneous V+V ligations are the key driver of sequence scrambling by linking oligomers from non-adjacent genomic loci.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C50-C56 describe the three ligation types and their roles in replication fidelity. These findings are supported by the kinetic modeling and simulation data presented in Figures 1-2, with clear mechanistic explanations for how V+V ligations cause sequence scrambling.

results.result: A trade-off exists between fidelity and yield in VCG replication. At low VCG concentrations, yield is low due to unproductive F+F ligations; at high concentrations, fidelity is compromised by erroneous V+V ligations. Replication efficiency can be maximized by increasing oligomer length and decreasing VCG concentration.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C57-C60, C213-C215, and C217 describe the fidelity-yield trade-off, supported by extensive modeling results shown in Figure 2. The adiabatic approach validates the simulation findings (C124), and analytical expressions (Equations 2-3) provide theoretical support.

results.result: Kinetic suppression of V+V ligations (by ensuring only monomers are reactive) breaks the fidelity-yield trade-off, enabling high fidelity and yield at arbitrarily high VCG concentrations. This suppression can be intrinsic to activation chemistry or externally imposed.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C61, C62, C179-C181, and C220 describe kinetic suppression as a solution to the fidelity-yield trade-off. This is supported by modeling results (Figure 6B) and experimental citations (Ding et al., 2022; Prywes et al., 2016) showing orders of magnitude differences in ligation rates.

results.result: Under kinetic suppression conditions at high VCG concentrations, shorter oligomers are extended by monomers more quickly than longer oligomers ('productivity inversion'). This phenomenon, observed experimentally by Ding et al. (2023), is explained by short oligomers sequestering long oligomers as templates while long oligomers cannot effectively use short oligomers as templates.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C14, C63-C65, C197, C199-C209, and C222-C224 describe productivity inversion. The model prediction (Figure 7B) is validated against experimental observations (Ding et al., 2023), and a mechanistic explanation is provided (Figure 7C-E). Semi-analytical expressions for threshold concentrations strengthen the theoretical foundation.

results.result: Longer VCG oligomers enable higher maximal replication efficiency, with the required oligomer length scaling logarithmically with genome size. The VCG scenario enables high-fidelity replication of long genomes (e.g., 1000 nt) using relatively short oligomers (e.g., 10 nt).
results.evaluation: Claims C127, C129, C132, C242, and C244 describe the relationship between oligomer length and replication efficiency. These are supported by modeling results (Figure 2G-H) and analytical approximations (Equation 3). The logarithmic scaling with genome size is mathematically derived.

results.result: In multi-length VCG pools, maximal replication efficiency is bounded by the efficiency of the longest oligomer in the pool, independent of shorter oligomers present. Including shorter oligomers has minimal effect on dominant ligation types.
results.evaluation: Claims C154, C155, C160, C162, and C218 describe the dominance of long oligomers in multi-length pools. This is supported by modeling results in Figures 3-4, showing that efficiency is governed by the longest oligomers due to their greater complex stability.

results.result: Including dimers as feedstock significantly reduces replication efficiency by enabling incorrect F+V ligations through dangling-end binding. The maximal efficiency with dimers remains below 100% and depends on dimer concentration, as described by an upper bound equation (Equation 4).
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C178 and C219 describe the negative impact of dimers on replication efficiency. This is supported by modeling results (Figure 5B-D) and analytical derivations (Equation 4, Appendix 3). The mechanism is clearly explained through complex stability analysis.

results.result: The authors developed a kinetic model incorporating (de)hybridization and templated ligation to characterize VCG replication across diverse pool compositions. The model uses Gillespie algorithm simulations and an adiabatic approximation method, with the latter validated against simulation data.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49, C69-C70, C86, C91-C95, C104, C111-C113, and C122-C124 describe the modeling methodology. The approach is well-documented in the Methods section, with validation shown in Figure 2B-D. The adiabatic approximation is justified by the timescale separation between hybridization and ligation.

results.result: The VCG constitutes a promising scenario for prebiotic information replication that could mitigate challenges in non-enzymatic copying, such as incomplete copies and high error rates. The circular genome structure eliminates the issue of incomplete copies since any subsequence is valid.
results.evaluation: Claims C15, C16, C40-C42 present conclusions about the VCG's promise for prebiotic replication. These are supported by the modeling results showing conditions for high-fidelity replication and the logical argument that circular genomes avoid incomplete copy problems. However, this remains a theoretical prediction requiring experimental validation.

results.result: The model makes several simplifying assumptions: instantaneous dehybridization with mismatches, uniform binding rates, and coarse-grained activation chemistry. While these simplifications may affect quantitative predictions, the model successfully reproduces experimental observations qualitatively.
results.evaluation: Claims C225-C238 acknowledge model limitations and their potential impacts. The authors provide reasonable justifications for why these simplifications are acceptable (e.g., terminal mismatches reduce ligation rates, C229) and demonstrate qualitative agreement with experiments (C238), supporting the model's validity despite its approximations.

results.result: Prior computational work by Chamanian and Higgs (2022) identified sequence scrambling as a vulnerability of the VCG scenario, and the spontaneous emergence of VCG pools is expected to be rare. The conditions preventing genome instability were previously unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 and C68 accurately cite and describe prior work by Chamanian and Higgs (2022). These claims establish the context and motivation for the current study, which addresses the previously unclear conditions for VCG stability.

results.result: Enzyme-free self-replication mechanisms before complex ribozymes remain elusive. Template-directed primer extension faces challenges including incomplete copies (≤12 nt added) and frequent errors due to limited thermodynamic discrimination, though some mitigation strategies exist.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C31 accurately summarize the state of the field regarding enzyme-free replication challenges, with appropriate citations to experimental work (Leveau et al., 2022; Kervio et al., 2010; Duzdevich et al., 2021; Göppel et al., 2021). These establish the scientific context for the VCG scenario.

results.result: While introducing multiple oligomer lengths might theoretically improve V+V ligation fidelity through long oligomers templating short oligomer ligation, this requires unrealistically strong binding affinity. When oligomers are similar in size, F+V ligations remain the most reliable mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C139, C141-C142, and C149-C152 describe the limited benefit of multi-length pools for improving V+V fidelity. This is supported by modeling results in Figure 3 and supplementary figures, showing that the theoretical improvement requires impractical binding strengths.

results.result: The oligomer length distribution arises from the interplay between chemical kinetics and environmental transport, creating an emergent length scale that shapes VCG replication. The constraints identified in this work can guide the search for self-replicating pools in the space of possible environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C251, C253, C256-C258 discuss the role of environmental factors in determining VCG pool composition and the implications for prebiotic scenarios. These are supported by citations (Rosenberger et al., 2021; Ianeselli et al., 2023) and logical reasoning about how environments select for genome properties.

results.result: The transition to living systems requires enzyme-free genetic replication. RNA is assumed to play a central role due to its dual capacity for information storage and catalysis. While progress has been made in understanding ribonucleotide formation and ribozyme function, a convincing scenario bridging prebiotic chemistry and ribozyme-catalyzed replication is missing.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C17-C19, C210-C212, and C239-C241 establish the scientific context with appropriate citations to foundational work in the RNA world hypothesis. These represent well-established knowledge in the field and properly frame the research problem.

results.result: The authors developed a kinetic model that explicitly incorporates association/dissociation of RNA strands and templated ligation to characterize VCG replication fidelity and yield. They used stochastic simulations based on the Gillespie algorithm and introduced an approximate adiabatic method assuming ligation is much slower than hybridization/dehybridization, which agrees well with simulation data.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly praise the kinetic model as 'carefully and realistically created' (Reviewer 3), 'high-quality theoretical modeling' (Reviewer 2), and presenting 'convincing theoretical arguments, simulations' (Editor/Reviewer 1). No concerns are raised about the modeling methodology.

results.result: The authors identify three competing types of ligation reactions in VCG pools: F+F ligations (producing short products), F+V ligations (typically correct), and V+V ligations (often erroneous). They find that erroneous V+V ligations are a key driver of sequence scrambling by linking oligomers from non-adjacent genomic loci, and that fidelity is determined by competition between correct F+V extension and erroneous V+V ligation. This creates a trade-off between fidelity and yield.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'additional limitations are identified. Specifically, it is shown that VCG is well replicated when the oligomers are elongated by sufficiently short chains from "feedstock" pool. However, ligation of oligomers from VCG itself results in a high error rate.' This directly supports the claims about the three ligation types and the fidelity-yield trade-off. No reviewer challenges these findings.

results.result: The authors find that replication efficiency can be optimized by increasing the length of VCG oligomers and reducing their concentration. Longer oligomers enable higher maxima in replication efficiency, and at higher temperatures VCG pools require longer oligomers to replicate with high efficiency. However, fidelity can be improved at the cost of reduced yield.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'the authors find that the length (longer is better) and concentration (intermediate is better) of the VCG oligos have an outsized impact on the fidelity and yield of VCG production with important implications for future VCG design.' This directly affirms these findings. No concerns are raised about these results.

results.result: The authors show that kinetic suppression of V+V ligations (such that each ligation incorporates only one monomer at a time) can break the fidelity-yield trade-off, enabling both high fidelity and yield at high VCG concentrations. This can be achieved through intrinsic properties of activation chemistry or by selectively activating only monomers.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly highlights this as a strength: 'They also identify that activation of only RNA monomers, which can be achieved using environmental separation of the activation and replication, can relax the constraints on the concentration of long VCG component oligos by avoiding the error-prone oligo-oligo ligation.' The reviewer further notes 'Fig. 6 outlines important constraints for scientists studying the origin of life. It supports the claim that the separation of activation and replication chemistry is required for efficient non-enzymatic replication.' No concerns are raised.

results.result: Under conditions of kinetic suppression, the model predicts that shorter oligomers are extended by monomers more quickly than long oligomers at high VCG concentrations. This phenomenon has been observed experimentally by Ding et al. (2023), and the authors provide a theoretical explanation based on asymmetric productive interactions: short oligomers can sequester long oligomers as templates, but not vice versa.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states this is 'Another strength of the work is that it explains why shorter oligos extend better compared to the long ones in complex VCG mixtures. This point is independent of the activation chemistry used (it simply depends on the kinetics and thermodynamics of RNA base-pairing) so it should be very generalizable.' The reviewer notes this 'has been observed experimentally (Ding et al., JACS 2023) but was unexplained rigorously until now.' No concerns are raised.

results.result: The authors find that including dimers as feedstock increases the error fraction because dimers that bind to a template with a dangling end are prone to form incorrect products. The maximal attainable efficiency is significantly lower for pools with dimers than without, and this sets an upper bound on replication efficiency that depends on dimer concentration in the feedstock.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges these findings about dimers. The results are presented as part of the systematic exploration of pool compositions, and the modeling approach has been validated by all reviewers. The claims are internally consistent with the overall framework.

results.result: When the pool contains VCG oligomers of multiple lengths, replication efficiency is typically governed by the longest oligomer in the pool. The maximal replication efficiency is always bounded by the efficiency of the longest VCG oligomer, independent of the presence or length of shorter oligomers.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges these findings. They are consistent with the overall modeling framework that has been validated by all reviewers. The claims follow logically from the competition between different ligation types.

results.result: The model suggests that the VCG scenario enables high-fidelity replication of long genomes, even in pools containing relatively short VCG oligomers. If oligomers exceed a minimum length (L_U^min) by about three nucleotides, accurate replication becomes feasible.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges this conclusion. Reviewer 1 (Editor) states the study presents 'convincing theoretical arguments' about 'potential features and limitations' of the VCG model. The conclusion follows from the validated modeling framework.

results.result: The authors cite prior work by Chamanian and Higgs (2022) showing that the VCG scenario is prone to sequence scrambling when the genome contains identical sequence motifs at multiple loci. It remains unclear which conditions could prevent this genome instability.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly asks '(1) It is not clear from the paper whether the observed error has the same nature as sequence scrambling' raised by Chamanian and Higgs. This indicates the relationship between the current work's findings and the prior sequence scrambling problem needs clarification.

results.result: The authors acknowledge several limitations of their coarse-grained model: it assumes instantaneous dehybridization with mismatches (though real duplexes tolerate some mismatches), simplifies hybridization dynamics, doesn't model activation chemistry explicitly, and may not fully capture nicked complex stability or gap-filling kinetics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'The kinetic model is carefully and realistically created' while also noting the authors 'describe the experimental setup well enough to qualitatively reproduce features observed in experiments.' The reviewers accept the coarse-grained approach as appropriate for the study's goals. Reviewer 2 raises a related concern about regime choice (point 4), but doesn't challenge the model assumptions directly.

results.result: Both characteristic lengths L_E^max and L_U^min scale logarithmically with genome size.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states '(2) The authors introduce two important lengths LS1 and LS2 only in the conclusions and do not explain enough which each of them is important. It would make sense to discuss this early in the manuscript.' This indicates the reviewers find the presentation of these characteristic lengths unclear and want better explanation of their importance.

results.result: For sufficiently short oligomers (up to about 11 nt), hybridization/dehybridization occur much faster than ligation, so binding equilibrates before ligation. Due to computational limitations, the authors calculate observables based on productive complex concentrations rather than waiting for actual ligation events.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises concern '(4) Furthermore, the problem has another important length, L0 that is never introduced or discussed: a minimal hybridization length with a lifetime longer than the ligation time. From the parameters given, it appears that L0 is sufficiently long (~10 bases). In other words, it appears that the study is done is a somewhat suboptimal regime: most hybridization events do not lead to a ligation.' This directly questions the regime choice and the adiabatic approximation's validity.

results.result: Peaked length distributions can emerge from the interplay of templated ligation, (de)hybridization, and outflux in open systems according to Rosenberger et al., 2021.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states '(3) It is not entirely clear why specific length distribution for VCG oligomers has to be assumed rather than emerged from simulations.' This questions why the length distribution is assumed rather than derived, suggesting the connection to emergent distributions needs clarification.
